statement: What is the time complexity of accessing an element in an array by its index?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
explanation: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, allowing direct index calculation in constant O(1) time.

statement: When capacity is available, what is the worst-case time complexity of inserting an element at the beginning of an array?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n log n)
explanation: Inserting at the beginning requires shifting all existing n elements one position to the right, taking O(n) time.

statement: Which memory layout property allows fast element access in an array?
options: Non-linear pointers
Contiguous memory allocation
Hash bucket indexing
Dynamic tree nodes
explanation: Contiguous memory allocation enables calculating memory addresses directly using base_address + index * element_size.

statement: What is the maximum number of elements an array of fixed size N can hold?
options: N
Unlimited
explanation: A fixed-size array of length N is allocated with exactly N memory slots.

statement: In zero-based indexing, what is the index of the last element in an array of size N?
options: N
explanation: Since indexing starts at 0, the Nth element is located at index N - 1.

statement: Why does deleting an element from the middle of an array take O(n) time in the worst case?
options: All elements after the deleted position must shift left
The array memory address is re-allocated
The array must be sorted after deletion
It requires converting elements to pointers
explanation: Deleting an element leaves a gap; all subsequent elements must shift left by one position to maintain contiguous storage.

statement: What is the worst-case time complexity of traversing every element in a 1D array of size N?
options: O(log N)
O(N²)
O(N)
explanation: Traversing requires visiting each of the N elements exactly once, taking linear O(N) time.

statement: Which array operation has O(1) time complexity when operating at the end of a dynamic array with available capacity?
options: Prepending an element at index 0
Appending an element at the last position
Inserting an element at index N / 2
Searching for an unindexed value
explanation: Appending at the end does not require shifting any existing elements, taking constant O(1) time when capacity is available.

statement: What is the worst-case time complexity of Linear Search on an unsorted array of size n?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
explanation: In the worst case, the target element is at the last index or not present at all, requiring n comparisons.

statement: Does Linear Search require the target array to be sorted before searching?
options: Yes, always
No, it works on unsorted arrays
Only if array size > 100
Yes, but only in descending order
explanation: Linear search checks elements sequentially one by one, so array order or sorting is not required.

statement: What is the best-case time complexity of Linear Search?
options: O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
explanation: The best case occurs when the target element is at the very first index (index 0), taking O(1) time.

statement: How many comparisons will Linear Search make if the target element is NOT present in an array of N items?
options: 0 comparisons
N comparisons
N / 2 comparisons
log2(N) comparisons
explanation: If the target is missing, Linear Search must check every single one of the N items before concluding it is absent.

statement: What is the average-case time complexity of Linear Search on an unsorted array?
options: O(log N)
O(N)
O(N²)
explanation: On average, Linear Search inspects roughly N / 2 elements, which simplifies to O(N) linear time in asymptotic analysis.

statement: Which scenario represents the BEST-case for Linear Search?
options: The target item is located at index 0
The target item is located at index N - 1
The array is pre-sorted in ascending order
The target item is not in the array
explanation: When the target is at index 0, Linear Search finds it on the very first comparison in O(1) time.

statement: What does Linear Search do when inspecting elements in an array?
options: It checks each element sequentially from index 0 until a match is found or the end is reached
It jumps directly to the midpoint of the array
It compares elements using a binary decision tree
It sorts the array in place before comparing values
explanation: Linear Search inspects elements one by one in sequential order, starting from index 0 until the target is located or the array ends.

statement: If the target item is located at index 4 of an array, how many comparisons will a standard Linear Search make to find it?
options: 1 comparison
4 comparisons
5 comparisons
10 comparisons
explanation: Linear Search inspects indices 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 in order, making a total of 5 comparisons to locate the target.

statement: What is the primary objective of a sorting algorithm?
options: To arrange elements in a specific order such as ascending or descending
To compress the memory footprint of an array
To remove all duplicate values from a dataset
To convert numerical values into text strings
explanation: Sorting reorganizes data into a defined order (ascending or descending), making lookup operations like Binary Search possible.

statement: Which elementary sorting algorithm repeatedly compares and swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order?
options: Selection Sort
Bubble Sort
Quick Sort
Heap Sort
explanation: Bubble Sort compares adjacent pairs (index i and i + 1) and swaps them if out of order, causing larger items to bubble to the end.

statement: What is the time complexity of Selection Sort in the best, average, and worst cases?
options: O(N) best, O(N²) worst
O(N log N) in all cases
O(N²) in all cases
O(1) best, O(N) worst
explanation: Selection Sort always scans the remaining unsorted subarray to find the minimum element in every pass, requiring O(N²) comparisons regardless of initial order.

statement: How does Insertion Sort build the sorted array?
options: By finding the overall minimum and swapping it to index 0
By taking one element at a time and inserting it into its correct position in the sorted region
By dividing the array into two halves recursively
By selecting random pivot elements
explanation: Insertion Sort maintains a sorted subarray on the left, shifting larger elements right to insert the current key into its proper position.

statement: After the first complete pass of Bubble Sort on an unsorted array, where is the largest element guaranteed to be located?
options: At index 0
At the last index of the array
At the exact midpoint of the array
It remains in its original starting position
explanation: In each pass of Bubble Sort, adjacent swaps cause the largest unsorted element to 'bubble up' to its final position at the end of the array.

statement: What is the worst-case time complexity of Bubble Sort on an array of N elements in reverse order?
options: O(N)
O(N²)
O(N log N)
explanation: When the array is in reverse order, Bubble Sort must make N - 1 passes with maximum swaps, resulting in O(N²) quadratic time complexity.

statement: What does it mean for a sorting algorithm to be 'adaptive'?
options: It changes its memory size dynamically at runtime
Its running time improves when given an input array that is already partially sorted
It converts between ascending and descending order automatically
It uses secondary storage when RAM is full
explanation: An adaptive algorithm like Insertion Sort takes advantage of existing order in the input, reducing comparisons/shifts to run near O(N) time.

statement: What is an 'in-place' sorting algorithm?
options: An algorithm that requires O(N²) auxiliary array space
An algorithm that sorts the elements within the original array requiring O(1) extra space
An algorithm that only works on pre-allocated linked lists
An algorithm that preserves duplicate key index positions
explanation: In-place sorting algorithms modify the input array directly without requiring significant additional memory allocations.

statement: What is the index of the first element in a typical array?
explanation: Arrays use zero-based indexing, so the first element is always stored at index 0.

statement: Why does inserting or deleting an element at an arbitrary index in an array have an O(n) worst-case time complexity?
options: Remaining elements must be shifted in memory to maintain contiguous order
The entire array must be converted to a linked list first
Arrays automatically double their size on every insertion
Memory pointers must be re-sorted after every deletion
explanation: Inserting or deleting an element requires shifting the surrounding elements in memory to maintain contiguous allocation, taking O(n) time in the worst case.

statement: What is the purpose of the index while traversing an array?
options: It identifies the current element
It changes the array size
It sorts the array
It deletes the current element
explanation: The index identifies the position of the element currently being visited during traversal.

statement: Why does inserting an element in the middle of an array take O(n) time?
options: Elements after the insertion index must shift right
The entire array must be sorted
Memory addresses are randomized
Array index lookup is O(n)
explanation: Inserting in the middle requires shifting all subsequent elements right by one position to create room.

statement: Which array operation has O(1) constant time complexity?
options: Accessing an element by index
Searching for an item in an unsorted array
Inserting an element in the middle
Deleting an element from the middle
explanation: Arrays use contiguous memory offsets, allowing instant O(1) element access directly by index.

statement: In algorithm analysis, what does the term 'target' refer to?
options: The specific element you are searching for
The size of the array
The total execution time
The last element in memory
explanation: The target is the specific value or element the search algorithm is looking to locate.

statement: What is the worst-case time complexity of Linear Search on an array of n items?
options: O(n)
O(log n)
O(n²)
explanation: In the worst case, Linear Search must check all n elements if the target is at the end or missing.

statement: What is the essential prerequisite for applying Binary Search to an array?
options: The array must be sorted
The array size must be even
All elements must be positive
The array must contain unique values
explanation: Binary Search relies on sorted order to eliminate half the search space at each comparison.

statement: When searching for target 72 in the sorted array [4, 12, 19, 27, 33, 44, 51, 60, 72, 81, 95], how many comparisons does Binary Search take compared to Linear Search?
options: 2 comparisons for Binary Search vs 9 comparisons for Linear Search
11 comparisons for Binary Search vs 1 comparison for Linear Search
5 comparisons for Binary Search vs 5 comparisons for Linear Search
1 comparison for Binary Search vs 11 comparisons for Linear Search
explanation: Binary Search inspects midpoint 44 and then midpoint 72 (2 comparisons), while Linear Search checks each item sequentially from 4 up to 72 (9 comparisons).

statement: What is the primary benefit of organizing data into a sorted order?
options: It enables faster search and lookup operations like Binary Search
It reduces the memory size of the array
It converts integers to strings automatically
It prevents duplicate elements from being added
explanation: Sorted order is required by algorithms like Binary Search, reducing search time from O(n) to O(log n).

statement: What is the best-case time complexity of Bubble Sort when an early-exit optimization is used on pre-sorted data?
options: O(n)
O(n²)
O(log n)
explanation: With an early-exit flag, Bubble Sort makes a single O(n) pass over pre-sorted data, detecting zero swaps and finishing early.

statement: Why does Selection Sort always have a time complexity of O(n²), even on already sorted data?
options: It must scan the entire unsorted region to find the minimum in every pass
It performs n² swaps in every pass
It doubles the array size at each step
It uses recursion to find the minimum
explanation: Selection Sort does not check if the array is already sorted; it unconditionally scans the remaining unsorted items to find the minimum in every pass.

statement: How does Insertion Sort perform when given an array that is already almost completely sorted?
options: It runs efficiently in near O(n) time with very few element shifts
It takes O(n²) time regardless of initial order
It throws an index out of bounds error
It requires O(n log n) additional memory
explanation: Insertion Sort is adaptive: if elements are already in order, it makes only 1 comparison per element and 0 shifts, taking O(n) time.

statement: Which elementary sorting algorithm minimizes the total number of element swaps to at most O(n)?
options: Selection Sort
Bubble Sort
Insertion Sort
Merge Sort
explanation: Selection Sort performs at most 1 swap per pass (n - 1 total swaps max), minimizing memory write operations.

statement: What is the primary purpose of a data structure?
options: To compress digital image files
To organize and store data efficiently for fast access and operations
To convert source code into machine language
To secure network connections against unauthorized access
explanation: Data structures provide organized formats for storing and managing data so that operations can be performed efficiently.

statement: An office should serve students in the order they arrive. Which structure directly models that rule?
options: A stack, because the newest student should be served first
A queue, because the earliest arrival should be served first
An array, because items must always be removed from the middle
A linked list, because it always gives direct access to any position
explanation: A queue follows first-in, first-out order: new arrivals join the back, and the earliest arrival is taken from the front. Other structures can store the same students, but the queue directly represents the required service order.

statement: What is an algorithm?
options: A physical hardware component inside a CPU
A step-by-step procedure or set of rules for solving a problem
A database table containing user records
An operating system user interface layout
explanation: An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions or rules designed to accomplish a specific task or solve a problem.

statement: An array grows from 4 items to 8. If you search for a value that is not present by checking each item in order, how does the number of comparisons change?
options: It stays at 1 comparison
It doubles from 4 comparisons to 8
It decreases from 8 comparisons to 4
It becomes 64 comparisons
explanation: A search for an absent value must check every item. With 4 items it makes 4 comparisons, and with 8 items it makes 8, so the comparisons double when the input size doubles in this example.

statement: In a singly linked list, what does the next reference of the final (tail) node point to?
options: The head node of the list
null (or nullptr / None), indicating the end of the list
The previous node in the list
Index 0 in memory
explanation: The tail node is the last element in a singly linked list, so its next reference is set to null (or nullptr / None) to signal that there are no further nodes.

statement: Why does accessing an element at position k in a singly linked list take O(n) worst-case time instead of O(1)?
options: The list must follow k sequential pointer references starting from the head node
All nodes must be re-sorted in memory before accessing position k
Linked lists automatically double their memory size during position access
Elements in a linked list are accessed using a binary search tree
explanation: Unlike arrays, linked lists do not store elements in contiguous memory slots, so direct index calculation is impossible. To reach position k, the list must traverse nodes sequentially starting from head.

statement: When inserting a new node after an existing node prev, why must you set newNode.next = prev.next BEFORE setting prev.next = newNode?
options: Updating prev.next first overwrites the only reference to the rest of the list, losing those nodes
Setting prev.next first triggers an automatic array memory reallocation error
Assigning newNode.next first sorts the list elements in ascending order
The next pointer of newNode must always point to the head node first
explanation: In a singly linked list, prev.next is the only pointer referencing the subsequent nodes. Overwriting prev.next before connecting newNode.next causes you to permanently lose access to the remaining nodes.

statement: Why does removing an interior node from a singly linked list require finding its predecessor node?
options: The predecessor's next pointer must be updated to point past the removed node to the subsequent node
The predecessor node stores the total size and capacity of the entire list
The predecessor node automatically shifts all subsequent array elements to the left
Singly linked lists can only delete nodes starting from the tail node
explanation: Because pointers flow only forward in a singly linked list, unlinking an interior node requires modifying the predecessor's next reference (prev.next = target.next) so it bypasses the deleted node.

statement: What is a key memory trade-off of a doubly linked list compared to a singly linked list?
options: Every node must store two pointer addresses (next and prev), increasing per-node memory overhead
Doubly linked lists store elements in contiguous memory slots like arrays
Doubly linked lists cannot perform O(1) head insertion
Nodes in a doubly linked list cannot store integer data values
explanation: Because each node in a doubly linked list contains both next and prev pointer references, it requires more memory per node than a singly linked list node which stores only a next pointer.

statement: In a singly linked list, how does a traversal algorithm determine that it has reached the end of the list?
options: The index variable reaches the fixed capacity limit N
The current node's next pointer equals null (or nullptr / None)
The node data value equals zero
The head reference is automatically set to null
explanation: In a singly linked list, the tail node's next pointer points to null (or nullptr / None), which signals that no further nodes exist in the chain.

statement: Why does accessing position k in a singly linked list take O(n) worst-case time?
options: The list must copy all n nodes into an array before reading position k
Position access requires sorting the entire list in ascending order
The list has no direct array-style index access, so reaching position k requires following links from head
The head pointer automatically doubles its memory size during position lookup
explanation: A singly linked list does not provide direct, array-style index access. To reach position k, you must follow links sequentially from head; in the worst case, reaching a position near the end requires traversing O(n) nodes.

statement: When inserting a new node after an existing node prevNode, why must you set newNode.next = prevNode.next BEFORE updating prevNode.next = newNode?
options: Assigning prevNode.next first causes an automatic memory allocation error in Java and Python
Setting newNode.next first automatically sorts the list elements
The newNode pointer must always point to the head node
Updating prevNode.next first overwrites the pointer referencing the rest of the list, losing access to subsequent nodes
explanation: In a singly linked list, prevNode.next is the only reference pointing to the rest of the list. Overwriting it first severs access to all remaining nodes.

statement: Why is locating the predecessor node (prev) necessary to remove an interior node target from a singly linked list?
options: The predecessor's next pointer must be updated (prev.next = target.next) to bypass the target node
The predecessor node stores the list's total capacity and element count
Singly linked lists can only delete nodes if they are located at index 0
The predecessor node automatically shifts remaining array items left
explanation: Singly linked list pointers flow forward only. Unlinking target requires finding prev so prev.next can be pointed past target to target.next.

statement: Which scenario represents a primary advantage of a singly linked list over a dynamic array?
options: Accessing an element at an arbitrary index k takes O(1) constant time
Inserting an element at the beginning (head) takes O(1) constant time without shifting existing elements
Elements occupy less memory per element because no pointers are needed
Binary search can be performed in O(log n) time without extra traversal
explanation: Inserting at the head of a linked list updates two pointer references in O(1) time, whereas prepending to an array requires shifting all n elements right in O(n) time.
